records.english: We hang the festival clothes in the shade so that the colours don't fade.
records.zomi: A rong a mial loh nadingin pawi puante limliam ah i vui uh hi.

records.english: When I wear the shawl my grandmother made, I feel as if she is still with me.
records.zomi: Ka pi' bawl puan ka silh ciangin amah kei tawh a om lai bangin ka kisa hi.

records.english: Where did you buy that beautiful shawl?
records.zomi: Tua puan hoih pen koi ah na lei hiam?

records.english: I didn't buy it; my grandmother wove it for me on her loom.
records.zomi: Ka lei kei hi; ka pi in a puan tahna tungah hong tahsak hi.

records.english: We mustn't sit on the woven cloth that covers the table at the ceremony.
records.zomi: Pawi ah dawhkan a khuh puan tah tungah i tu kei ding uh hi.

records.english: My cousin sells hand-woven bags online to people who have moved far from home.
records.zomi: Ka sanggam in khut tawh tah ip te inn pan gamla-a pai khin mite kiangah online-in a zuak hi.

records.english: Wrap the cloth twice around your waist and tuck the end in firmly.
records.zomi: Na kawng ah puan nihvei tuam inla a tawp kipte-in sel in.

records.english: My mother wears her woven wrap skirt to church every Sunday.
records.zomi: Ka nu in Nipini simin pawlpi ah a puannial tah a silh hi.

records.english: My aunt is teaching me to weave on a small loom that she keeps on the veranda.
records.zomi: Ka ni in a inn mai-a a koih puan tahna neu khat tungah puan tah hong sinsak hi.

records.english: Thank you for lending me your wrap skirt for the dance.
records.zomi: Lam adingin na puannial hong leitawi sak manin ka lungdam hi.

records.english: At the festival, the older women walked slowly between the stalls, looking closely at every piece of cloth.
records.zomi: Pawi ah numei upate in van zuakna mun kikal-ah nuam takin a kal uh a, puan khempeuh a en kicing uh hi.

records.english: Would you help me fold this long skirt so that it fits in my suitcase?
records.zomi: Hih puannial sau ka van bawm sungah a lut theih nadingin hong khupsak thei ding na hi hiam?

records.english: Please don't put the woven skirt in the washing machine; wash it gently by hand.
records.zomi: Puannial tah puan sawpna seet sungah koih kei inla, khut tawh nem takin sawp in.

records.english: Weaving at home was once a skill that almost every girl in our village was expected to learn.
records.zomi: Inn ah puan tah pen i khua-a numei naupang khempeuh in a sin dingin kilamen siamna khat ahi ngei hi.

records.english: Everyone, please come in your traditional clothes for the group photo on Sunday.
records.zomi: Mi khempeuh, Nipini-a pawl lim adingin ngeina puan tawh hong pai un.

records.english: Hand-woven cloth takes so long to make that a single piece can represent weeks of careful work.
records.zomi: Khut tawh tah puan bawl hun a sawt mahmah ahih manin puan khat in kal tampi sung limtak-a nasep a lak thei hi.

records.english: Can you show me which way the pattern is supposed to face?
records.zomi: Puan lim koi lam ah a nga ding hiam hong lak thei ding na hi hiam?

records.english: My sister made me practise wearing the long skirt before the wedding, so that I wouldn't trip on the steps.
records.zomi: Kahlei tungah ka khem loh nadingin mopawi ma-in ka u numei in puannial sau silh hong sinsak hi.

records.english: Is this shawl for everyday use, or is it only for special occasions?
records.zomi: Hih puan ni simin zat ding ahi hiam, ni tuam bek adingin ahi hiam?

records.english: The bride and groom both wore traditional clothes for the ceremony and changed for the evening party.
records.zomi: Mopawi pawi ah moneu leh mopa in ngeina puan a silh uh a, nitak kipahna adingin a kheel uh hi.

records.english: These patterns have been passed down from mother to daughter in our family for generations.
records.zomi: Hih puan limte i innkuan ah khangkhat khit khangkhat nu pan tanu kiangah kipia khia hi.

records.english: Put the new skirt on, and let's see whether it fits.
records.zomi: Puannial thak silh inla, a kilawm hiam i en ni.

records.english: Our neighbour had her wedding shawl repaired by an old weaver in the next village.
records.zomi: I innveng in a mopawi puan a kiang khua-a puan tah upa khat kiangah a phuaksak hi.

records.english: When our community held a fashion show, the young people mixed traditional cloth with modern styles.
records.zomi: I mipi in puan silh lakna a bawl ciangin khangnote in ngeina puan leh tulai silh dan a kihel sak uh hi.

records.english: Iron the shawl on the inside, so that the pattern isn't flattened.
records.zomi: Puan lim a kiphek loh nadingin puan a sung lam pan meisek in.

records.english: How long does it take to weave a whole skirt?
records.zomi: Puannial khat tah dingin hun bangzah a la hiam?

records.english: For my mother, about a month, if she weaves every evening.
records.zomi: Ka nu adingin, nitak simin a tah leh kha khat bang.

records.english: Who taught you to tie the head wrap like that?
records.zomi: Tua bangin lu tuam tuam dan kua in hong sinsak hiam?

records.english: My grandfather was buried in the traditional shirt he wore at his wedding.
records.zomi: Ka pu in a mopawi ni-a a silh ngeina puan tawh kivui hi.

records.english: The shawl's edges were finished with a tiny knot every few centimetres.
records.zomi: Puan' a gei te centimeter tawmno simin khau thuah neu khat tawh kizo hi.

records.english: I wore my traditional clothes to an international evening at university, and people asked me about them all night.
records.zomi: Sangpi ah gamdang mite' nitak kikhopna khat ah ka ngeina puan ka silh a, mite in zan bup a tungtang hong dong uh hi.

records.english: Machine-made copies of traditional cloth are cheaper, but many people can tell the difference at once.
records.zomi: Seet tawh bawl ngeina puan a man neem zaw a, ahi zongin mi tampi in a kibatlohna a thei pah uh hi.

records.english: Traditional clothes are heavier than jeans, but they're warm on cold mornings.
records.zomi: Ngeina puan jeans sangin a gik zaw a, ahi zongin zingsang vot ciangin a lum hi.

records.english: Wearing traditional clothes for the first time at a big festival can make a child feel very grown up.
records.zomi: Pawi lianpi khat ah a masa pen-in ngeina puan silh in naupang khat a upa mahmah bangin a kisak sak thei hi.

records.english: Fewer young people are learning to weave, so some families are worried that the skills will be lost.
records.zomi: Khangnote tawmno bek in puan tah a sin uh ahih manin innkuan pawl khat in siamnate a mang ding ci-in a lungkham uh hi.

records.english: You two can share the shawl, since there's only one left in the chest.
records.zomi: Bawm sungah khat bek a om lai ahih manin na nih in puan na kihawm thei uh hi.

records.english: Do men in your family wear traditional clothes too?
records.zomi: Na innkuan-a pasalte in zong ngeina puan a silh uh hiam?

records.english: Some families keep a set of traditional clothes for each child, so that everyone is ready for the festival.
records.zomi: Innkuan pawl khat in pawi adingin mi khempeuh a kiginkhol nadingin naupang khatciat adingin ngeina puan tuam a kem uh hi.

records.english: Traditional clothing is not frozen in the past; each generation adds new colours and small changes.
records.zomi: Ngeina puan pen hun bei sungah a khang lo bang hi lo a; khangthak khempeuh in rong thakte leh kikheelna neunote a behlap uh hi.

records.english: Choosing what to wear to a wedding can be harder when you have to respect both families' traditions.

records.english: We used a wooden comb to press each new thread tightly against the last.
records.zomi: Khau thak khempeuh a nunung pen tawh a kip takin nek dingin sing tawh bawl puan tahna vanzat khat i zang uh hi.

records.english: You need a strong thread for the edges, or the cloth will start to come apart.
records.zomi: A gei te adingin khau hat na kisam a, a kisam kei leh puan a kiphel kipan ding hi.

records.english: How do you keep the colours so bright after so many years?
records.zomi: Kum tampi khit ciangin rongte bangci-in na taangsak lai hiam?

records.english: The colours a family chooses for its cloth can carry meanings that only older relatives fully understand.

records.english: Children, keep your festival clothes clean until the photos have been taken.
records.zomi: Naupangte, lim kilak ma-in na pawi puante uh siangtho takin kem un.

records.english: This skirt is too long for me, so my aunt will shorten it.
records.zomi: Hih puannial kei adingin a sau lua ahih manin ka ni in a tomsak ding hi.

records.english: My grandmother keeps her best shawls folded in a wooden chest with dried leaves to keep insects away.
records.zomi: Ka pi in a puan hoih pente puan siasak thei ganhing neuneute a pelh nadingin sing bawm sungah a keu teh nate tawh a khup-in a kem hi.

records.english: My mother had a jacket made for me from the same cloth as her own.
records.zomi: Ka nu in amah' puan kibang mah tawh kei adingin jacket khat a bawlsak hi.

records.english: In our family, traditional clothes are kept for weddings, festivals and other special days.
records.zomi: I innkuan ah ngeina puan mopawi, pawi leh ni tuam dangte adingin kikem hi.

records.english: Why are you wearing your traditional clothes today?
records.zomi: Bang hangin tuni-in na ngeina puan na silh hiam?

records.english: It's my grandparents' fiftieth wedding anniversary.
records.zomi: Ka pu leh pi' kiteenna kum sawmnga cinna ni ahi hi.

records.english: A good shawl can last for decades if it is stored carefully and washed only when necessary.
records.zomi: Puan hoih khat limtakin kikem-a a kisam ciang bek-a kisawp leh kum sawm tampi a zang thei hi.

records.english: My father has a traditional shirt that he wears only for funerals and memorial services.

records.english: Each stripe on the cloth is woven in by hand, one thread at a time.
records.zomi: Puan tung-a zial khempeuh khut tawh khau khat zawh khat kitah hi.

records.english: I really do love the deep red of this old skirt.
records.zomi: Hih puannial lui' sansiang nawng ka it taktak hi.

records.english: When young people living abroad wear traditional clothes at a festival, it can be a quiet way of saying where they come from.
records.zomi: Gamdang-a teeng khangnote in pawi khat ah ngeina puan a silh uh ciangin amau koi pan hong pai uh hiam a gen dan dai khat a hi thei hi.

records.english: Can I borrow your traditional jacket for the cultural evening at school?

records.english: My little brother refuses to wear the traditional jacket because he says it's itchy.

records.english: Why must we always visit Grandma on Sundays?
records.zomi: Bang hangin Nipini simin Pi i veh tawntung kul uh hiam?

records.english: Why don't you want to go to your cousin's birthday party?
records.zomi: Bang hangin na sanggam' pianni kipahna ah pai na nuam kei hiam?

records.english: When parents can't give a reason for a rule, children quickly stop respecting it.
records.zomi: Nu leh pate in thukham khat adingin a hang a pia thei kei uh ciangin naupangte in manlang takin a zahtak nawn kei uh hi.

records.english: Why did you and Mum decide to move to the city?
records.zomi: Bang hangin nang leh Nu in khuapi ah pai dingin na khensat uh hiam?

records.english: We wanted you to be closer to a good school and a hospital.
records.zomi: Sang hoih leh damdawi inn tawh na kinai zawk nadingin i deih uh hi.

records.english: Children who are given honest reasons for family decisions usually cope with them better.
records.zomi: Innkuan thukhennate adingin a hang dik kipia naupangte in a tamzaw-in hoih zaw takin a thuak zo uh hi.

records.english: My son asked me, "Why do you go to work if you'd rather stay at home with us?"
records.zomi: Ka tapa in, “Eite tawh inn ah om na deih zaw leh bang hangin nasep ah na pai hiam?” hong ci hi.

records.english: I asked my parents why they had chosen to live so far from their own families.
records.zomi: Ka nu leh ka pa kiangah bang hangin amau' innkuan pan gamla mahmah ah teng dingin a teel uh hiam ka dong hi.

records.english: Why do you keep all these old letters?
records.zomi: Bang hangin hih lai lui khempeuh na kem hiam?

records.english: They're from your grandfather, and his handwriting reminds me of him.
records.zomi: Na pu' lai ahi a, a laigelh in amah hong phawksak hi.

records.english: Why don't you speak your parents' language at home?

records.english: My father never told us why he had stopped going to church, and we never dared to ask.

records.english: Why did you leave your job at the bank?
records.zomi: Bang hangin bank-a na nasep na nusia hiam?

records.english: I wanted to spend more time with my children while they were small.

records.english: Why isn't Dad eating with us tonight?
records.zomi: Bang hangin tu nitak Pa eite tawh ne lo hiam?

records.english: Why won't Grandpa talk about his time in the army?

records.english: Some memories are too painful, and he'd rather keep them to himself.

records.english: Why must I wear a jacket if I'm not cold?

records.english: Why shouldn't I tell my friends about our family's problems?

records.zomi: Bang hangin na lupna khan' a dang lam ah na suan hiam?

records.english: The morning sun kept waking me up.

records.english: Why are all the curtains closed in the middle of the day?
records.zomi: Bang hangin sunlai ah tukkhuak puan khempeuh kikhak hiam?

records.english: Your grandfather has a headache and needs to sleep.
records.zomi: Na pu in a lu a na a, ihmu kisam hi.

records.english: It took me years to understand why my mother worked two jobs without complaining and still said she was lucky.
records.zomi: Bang hangin ka nu in phun lo-in nasep nih a sem a, kampha ka hi hi, a ci lai hiam theih dingin kum tampi ka zang hi.

records.english: My daughter wants to know why she can't have a phone yet.
records.zomi: Bang hangin phone a nei thei nai lo hiam ka tanu in a theih nuam hi.

records.english: My grandmother asked me why I had cut my hair so short, and then said it suited me.

records.english: Why can't we have a dog?
records.zomi: Bang hangin ui i khawi thei kei hiam?

records.english: Our flat is too small, and nobody is at home during the day.
records.zomi: I inn a neu lua a, sunlai-in kuamah inn ah om lo hi.

records.english: Grandpa never explained why he always kept a small bag packed by the front door, and nobody liked to ask.
records.zomi: Bang hangin kongkhak mai ah ip neu khat a kicing-in a koih tawntung hiam Pu in a genteh ngei kei a, kuamah in dot a nuam kei uh hi.

records.english: Why does Grandma always set an extra place at the table?
records.zomi: Bang hangin Pi in dawhkan ah mun behlap khat a koih tawntung hiam?

records.english: What's the reason you changed your surname?
records.zomi: Na innkuan min na kheelna hang bang ahi hiam?

records.english: I took my husband's name when we married, as my mother did.
records.zomi: I kiteen ciangin ka nu bangin ka pasal' min ka la hi.

records.english: Why have you been so tired lately?
records.zomi: Bang hangin tu laitakin gim mahmah na hi hiam?

records.english: The baby has been waking up three times a night.

records.english: Why are you so quiet this evening?
records.zomi: Bang hangin tu nitak na dai mahmah hiam?

records.english: I had an argument with my best friend, and I don't want to talk about it yet.

records.english: I never asked my parents why they had married so young, and now that they're both gone, I wish I had.
records.zomi: Bang hangin naupang lai-in kiteen uh hiam ka nu leh ka pa ka dong ngei kei a, tu-in a nih in a sih khit uh ciangin ka dot ka deih hi.

records.english: Is there a reason you've stopped visiting your uncle?
records.zomi: Na pa neu na veh nawn lohna hang khat a om hiam?

records.english: We had a disagreement about money, and neither of us has phoned since.
records.zomi: Sum thu ah i kituak kei uh a, tua pan i nih in i kisam nawn kei uh hi.

records.english: Sometimes a child keeps asking why simply because they want the conversation to continue.
